summary: Strong, well-structured report arguing against shipping, with relevant cases and a clear conclusion. You achieved Excellent for C1, Very good for C2–C4, and Good for C5. Stakeholder analysis is broad rather than systematic, references are incomplete, no visuals are used, and some recommendation/EACE logic is inconsistent. Focus next on systematic stakeholder recommendations, stronger evidence and references, and visual/format improvements.
next_steps: Expand stakeholder analysis: create a structured section or table that systematically addresses each stakeholder's interests, risks, and decision-making recommendations, moving beyond broad mentions to meet Excellent for C2 and C3.

Strengthen evidence and references: add quantitative data, replace speculative claims (e.g., competitor-will-ship) with sourced evidence, and fix reference list issues ([3] URL, [1] malformed URL, [4] author formatting) to reach Excellent for C4.

Improve format and logic: add at least one visual element (stakeholder map or decision matrix), proofread for language slips, and revise the Recommendation to focus on refusing sign-off and escalating rather than refusing the contract; correct the EACE 2.3b misapplication and align the QA window with your earlier reasoning.

criteria.C1: You achieved Excellent. Your Introduction clearly identifies the core ethical dilemma, links it to engineering design and organisational competitive context, and lists stakeholders (Rachel, company, chip contractor, health department). To maintain this level, ensure your later stakeholder analysis remains as systematic as your introduction; currently it becomes broad rather than deep. Continue signposting several ethical concerns explicitly.
criteria.C2: Very good (8/10). Your 'To Ship or Not to Ship' section balances for/against arguments, and 'The Most Ethical Path' concludes clearly. For Excellent, extend recommendations to several distinct stakeholders—not just Rachel/company—and show how each should decide. Revise 'Recommendation': refusing the contract may exceed Rachel's authority; focus on refusing sign-off and escalating, and align the QA window with your earlier point that six months is too short.
criteria.C3: Very good (8/10). Your report is logically structured; 'The Most Ethical Path' and 'Conclusion' support the no-ship decision. For Excellent, demonstrate a systematic understanding of ethical issues for all stakeholders—currently your analysis is sound but not stakeholder-by-stakeholder. Consider a table or structured section mapping each stakeholder's interests, risks, and decision criteria. Also ensure every argument links explicitly to the conclusion.
criteria.C4: Very good (8/10). You use relevant cases (HSSIB, Volkswagen) and some quantitative detail, plus the Engineers Australia code. For Excellent, strengthen evidence: add both qualitative and quantitative data, and ensure references are complete and consistent—[3] lacks a URL, [1] has a malformed URL, [4] has poor author formatting. Replace the speculative competitor-will-ship argument with sourced evidence, and note the HSSIB case is analogous, not direct proof.
criteria.C5: Good (6/10). Sections serve their functions and writing is generally fluent, but there are language slips, no visual elements, and references are incomplete/inconsistent. For Very good, eliminate incorrect language uses, add several types of visual elements (e.g., stakeholder map, decision matrix) used competently, and provide a complete, consistently formatted reference list. Proofread carefully and ensure every reference supports your motivations.
